topics.title: Score-aware quantization (ScaNN)
topics.what_it_is: Standard quantization minimises the vector error. ScaNN weighs the error more along the direction of the vector, because that is the part that changes inner-product ranking.
topics.why: It gives better recall at the same code size for inner-product search.
steps: Split the quantisation error into parallel and orthogonal parts.
Penalise the parallel part more.
Train codebooks with this loss.
Search with lookup tables, then rerank.
trade_offs: Gains depend on data and metric.

worked_example.spec: Not run.

topics.title: Bi-encoder retrieval: encode the corpus once, the query at run time
topics.what_it_is: A bi-encoder embeds every passage offline and the query online. Search is the nearest vectors to the query vector by dot product or cosine. RAG (Lewis 2020) uses a DPR retriever over a Wikipedia index.
topics.why: This is the base of dense RAG: the expensive encoding happens once, query time needs one encoding and one index search.
steps: Encode all passages with E_P and index them.
At query time encode q with E_Q.
Search the index for the top-k.
Pass the passages to the generator.
trade_offs: Index and query encoders must match.
One vector per passage can miss exact terms: add BM25 (hybrid).

worked_example.spec: Existing real run: runs/ contains dense retrieval top-20 for 24 questions on 138 passages.

topics.title: Chunking: the map of strategies
topics.what_it_is: Chunking cuts a document into pieces that are embedded and retrieved. Strategies differ in what decides a cut: a count (fixed, sliding window), a separator list (recursive), a sentence boundary, a meaning shift (semantic), the document structure, an LLM, or a hierarchy (parent-child, tree).
topics.why: A chunk is the unit of retrieval and the unit of context given to the LLM. Too small: the answer is split and context is lost. Too large: the vector blurs several topics and the prompt fills with noise.

io.output: list of chunks with offsets and metadata

steps: Choose the unit: tokens, sentences, sections, propositions.
Choose the cut rule and the overlap.
Choose the embedded text versus the returned text (small-to-big).
Attach metadata and parent ids.
Measure: retrieval recall and answer quality at several sizes.
trade_offs: No size wins everywhere: the chunk-size test on real text below shows the sentence recall peak at 120 words, and top-1 hit rate flat within noise.
Semantic chunking costs embeddings at ingest and has not beaten fixed-size chunks consistently (Qu 2024).
The best chunk size depends on the query type (fact lookup versus summary).

worked_example.spec: Use the existing real chunk-size experiment: 15 full Wikipedia articles, all-MiniLM-L6-v2, whole-sentence chunks, no overlap, 20 questions, top-5 chunks.
worked_example.caveat: 20 questions: differences of 0.05 are one question; lexical proxy for the answer sentence; demo scale, not an evaluation.

topics.title: Cleaning text and attaching metadata
topics.what_it_is: Cleaning removes boilerplate (menus, headers, page numbers), repairs hyphenation and Unicode, and fixes encoding. Metadata is information attached to each chunk: source, page, section path, date, language, access rights.
topics.why: Metadata lets the retriever filter (date, source, tenant) and lets the answer cite its source. Boilerplate text creates near-identical vectors that crowd out real content.

io.output: clean text plus a metadata record per chunk

steps: Strip repeated headers, footers and navigation.
Normalise Unicode and whitespace; join hyphenated line breaks.
Detect the language per block.
Attach source id, page, heading path, timestamp, version.
Store metadata next to the vector so filters run at query time.
trade_offs: Over-cleaning deletes useful tokens (units, codes).
Metadata must be set at ingest; adding it later means re-processing.

worked_example.spec: Real-example passages already carry article, url, oldid, section, retrieved date and licence (data/corpus.json): show them as the metadata record of each chunk.

topics.title: Contextual retrieval (LLM context prefix per chunk)
topics.what_it_is: For each chunk an LLM writes a short context that places the chunk in its document ('This chunk is from the 2023 annual report, section on revenue'). The context is prepended before embedding and before BM25 indexing.
topics.why: A chunk such as 'revenue grew 3%' has no company or year. The prefix restores them, so the vector and keyword index can match.
steps: For each chunk, send the document (cached) and the chunk to an LLM.
Get a 50-100 token context.
Embed context+chunk and index it in BM25 too.
Optionally rerank.
trade_offs: One LLM call per chunk; prompt caching makes it cheaper.
Gains were measured by the vendor on its own datasets; independent evidence not found in this pass.

worked_example.spec: Not run: needs an LLM. A local-model test on 20 real chunks is a phase-2 option.

topics.title: How embedding models are trained (contrastive learning)
topics.what_it_is: The model is trained so that a query and its relevant passage get close vectors, and other passages get far vectors. The loss compares one positive with many negatives (in-batch and mined).
topics.why: The training objective decides what 'similar' means. A model trained for paraphrase may fail on question-to-answer retrieval.

formulas.verified: verified: softmax-over-negatives family confirmed in InfoNCE Eq. 4, DPR loss and E5 Eq. 2 (tau=0.01); the single formula shown is the common form, not a verbatim equation

steps: Collect or generate pairs (supervised QA, weak web pairs, or augmented views).
Encode both sides in a batch.
Treat other items in the batch as negatives.
Minimise the loss.
Evaluate on MTEB/BEIR.
trade_offs: Large batches give more negatives but need memory.
False negatives (a relevant passage labelled negative) hurt.
Weak-supervision data from the web carries bias.

worked_example.spec: Toy: compute the loss on the real 6-sentence cosine matrix in vectors_sample.json with s1 as query and s2 as positive (cos 0.5408), the other 4 as negatives, tau=0.05; recompute in Python in phase 2. Numbers are not stored here.

topics.title: Deduplication (exact, near-duplicate, semantic)
topics.what_it_is: Deduplication removes repeated documents or chunks. Exact dedup compares hashes. Near-duplicate dedup compares sets of shingles with MinHash or bit signatures with SimHash. Semantic dedup compares embeddings.
topics.why: Duplicates fill the top-k with the same content, waste index space, and bias counts. Lee et al. show that duplicates in training text cause memorisation; the same text in a corpus also biases retrieval.

io.output: set of chunks with duplicates removed or clustered

symbols.h_min: minimum of a random hash over a set

formulas.verified: NOT verified: Broder 1997 PDF is paywalled (IEEE); only the attribution is confirmed (Lee 2021 cites MinHash to Broder 1997)
NOT verified: Charikar 2002 PDF is paywalled (ACM)

steps: Cut each chunk into k-word shingles.
Compute n MinHash values per chunk.
Group chunks with equal values in some band (LSH).
Verify candidates with exact Jaccard or cosine.
Keep one chunk per group; keep the source ids of the others.
trade_offs: Threshold choice: too low removes legitimate variants (versions of a policy).
Near-duplicates with different dates may both matter: dedup by version, not by text.
Semantic dedup is O(n^2) without an index.

worked_example.spec: Run MinHash (datasketch) over the 138 passages and over overlap-chunked windows; report how many pairs exceed Jaccard 0.5. Recompute in Python; the pack has no duplicates by construction, so expect none from passages and many from 50%-overlap windows (prediction, to be measured).

topics.demo_hint: Slider: shingle size and band count versus duplicates found.

topics.title: DiskANN: a graph index on SSD for billion-scale data
topics.what_it_is: DiskANN builds a Vamana graph and stores full vectors on SSD, with compressed (PQ) vectors in RAM. A search uses the RAM codes to steer and reads few SSD pages to check.
topics.why: It serves very large collections on one machine with low memory.

io.output: approximate top-k with few disk reads

steps: Build the Vamana graph with pruned edges.
Keep PQ codes in RAM and full vectors with neighbour lists on SSD.
Greedy search guided by PQ distances.
Rerank the final candidates with full vectors read from SSD.
trade_offs: Disk latency sets the floor.
Static graph: updates need FreshDiskANN.

topics.title: Parsing documents (PDF, HTML, Office) into text with structure
topics.what_it_is: A parser reads a file and returns text plus structure: headings, lists, tables, figures and reading order. A PDF stores glyph positions, not paragraphs, so the parser must rebuild the order. Modern parsers use layout models and table-structure models.
topics.why: RAG can only retrieve what the parser keeps. A broken table or a wrong reading order puts wrong text into a chunk, and no embedding model can repair it.

io.output: structured document (Markdown or JSON) with element types and page coordinates

steps: Detect the file type and extract the text layer, or run OCR when there is none.
Run a layout model to find blocks (title, paragraph, table, figure, footnote).
Run a table-structure model on each table region.
Sort blocks into reading order.
Export Markdown or a document tree with metadata (page, bbox, heading path).
trade_offs: Multi-column layouts and footnotes break reading order.
Tables lose their row and column meaning when flattened.
Scanned pages need OCR; its errors flow into every later stage.
Speed versus fidelity: heavy layout models cost seconds per page.

worked_example.spec: Convert one PDF page with markitdown (fast) and with docling (layout + tables); diff the Markdown. No numbers invented: the demo reports what the tools return. topics.title: Embedding levels: word, sentence, document, multi-vector, sparse
topics.what_it_is: Word embeddings give one vector per word type (word2vec). Contextual models give one vector per token occurrence. Sentence and passage models give one vector per text span. Multi-vector models keep one vector per token. Sparse models give a vector over the vocabulary with few non-zero weights.
topics.why: The level sets what is compared and how: single-vector cosine is cheapest; multi-vector gives finer matching at larger storage; sparse keeps exact-term matching.

io.output: 1 vector, n vectors or a sparse vector

steps: Word level: lookup table learned by predicting context words.
Token level: transformer output per token.
Span level: pool token vectors (previous topic).
Multi-vector: keep all token vectors (ColBERT).
Sparse: project to vocabulary and keep top weights (SPLADE).
trade_offs: Word vectors have one vector per word, so 'bank' has a single meaning.
Documents longer than the token limit need chunking or hierarchical pooling.

worked_example.spec: Storage per level for the real passages (138, mean ~83 words): single-vector 384 floats each; multi-vector ~ number of tokens x 128 dims (ColBERT). Compute tokens with the tokenizer in phase 2.

topics.title: Text embedding: tokenisation to transformer to pooling to normalisation
topics.what_it_is: A text embedding model turns a string into one fixed-size vector. Steps: tokenise; run the transformer to get one contextual vector per token; pool the token vectors into one (mean or [CLS]); normalise to length 1. Similar meaning gives nearby vectors.
topics.why: The vector is what the index stores and what the query is compared with. The model, the pooling and the normalisation must be the same at ingest and at query time.

io.input: text (up to the token limit, 512 for many models)
io.output: vector of d floats (384 for all-MiniLM-L6-v2)

symbols.m_t: attention mask (1 for real token, 0 for padding)

formulas.verified: verified in part: SBERT Section 3 default is MEAN pooling; the mask-weighted form is the library implementation, not printed in the paper
verified: identity (cosine of unit vectors is their dot product)

steps: Tokenise and add special tokens.
Run the encoder: n tokens to n vectors of d numbers.
Pool with the attention mask.
L2-normalise.
Store; at query time repeat with the same model.
trade_offs: Mean pooling and [CLS] are not interchangeable: use the pooling the model was trained with.
Texts over the limit are truncated.
The query and document may need prefixes (E5 uses 'query: ' and 'passage: ').

worked_example.spec: REAL numbers in vectors_sample.json (all-MiniLM-L6-v2, d=384): raw vector norm of sentence s1 is 3.5581 (recomputed from the raw vector: 3.5581); the normalised vector has squared norm 1.0000 (recomputed 0.999995); cosine(s1,s2)=0.5408 (recomputed from the stored normalised vectors; stored matrix 0.54079).

topics.title: Exact (flat) search
topics.what_it_is: A flat index stores all vectors and compares the query with every one. It is exact: no approximation error.
topics.why: It is the correct baseline for recall and the right choice up to about hundreds of thousands of vectors.
steps: Compute all N similarities (matrix multiply).
Select the top-k (partial sort).
trade_offs: Time grows linearly with N.

topics.title: Filtered vector search (metadata, access rights)
topics.what_it_is: Real queries add conditions: date, source, tenant. Filtering after search may leave fewer than k results; filtering before search makes graph indexes disconnected. Filtered indexes handle both.

For selective filters use a filtered graph index (Filtered-DiskANN) or a predicate-agnostic one (ACORN).
Measure recall at the filter selectivity you expect.
trade_offs: Low selectivity (few matches) hurts graph indexes most.
Access rules must be applied at retrieval, not by the LLM.

topics.title: Fixed-size chunking (tokens or words)
topics.what_it_is: Cut the text every N tokens (or words), with or without overlap. It ignores meaning and is the baseline.
topics.why: It is the simplest and fastest option and the usual baseline in studies. DPR used fixed 100-word passages for the Wikipedia index.

formulas.verified: arithmetic, recomputed in Python on the real corpus

steps: Tokenise.
Slide a window of N with stride S=N-O.
Decode each window to text.
Embed and index.
trade_offs: Cuts sentences and tables in half.
Overlap protects boundary facts but raises the number of chunks and the cost.

worked_example.spec: Count chunks on the real corpus: 138 passages, 11,516 words in total (recomputed). Windows of 40 words: stride 40 gives 342 chunks; stride 30 (10-word overlap) gives 423 chunks, +23.7% index size (recomputed 2026-10-09 from corpus.json word counts).

topics.title: Hard negatives and negative mining
topics.what_it_is: A hard negative is a passage that looks relevant but is not. Training with them teaches the model fine differences. They come from BM25, from the model's own earlier index (ANCE), or from a stronger cross-encoder (RocketQA).
topics.why: Random negatives are too easy: the model learns little. Hard negatives bring most of the quality gain in dense retrieval.
steps: Retrieve top-k for each training query with BM25 or the current model.
Remove the known positives (and, with a cross-encoder, likely false negatives).
Add the rest as negatives in the loss.
Refresh the index periodically (ANCE).
trade_offs: False negatives: unlabelled relevant passages in the top-k. RocketQA denoises with a cross-encoder.
Index refresh during training is expensive.

worked_example.spec: Real example: for a pack question, list the top-20 of BM25 (runs/bm25.json) minus gold passages as candidate hard negatives and mark which look relevant by eye.

topics.title: Hierarchical / tree index (RAPTOR)
topics.what_it_is: Embed chunks, cluster them, have an LLM summarise each cluster, then repeat on the summaries. The result is a tree: leaves are chunks, upper nodes are summaries. Retrieval can search all levels.
topics.why: Broad questions need information from many chunks. Summary nodes answer them without reading every leaf.

io.output: multi-level tree of chunks and summaries

steps: Embed leaf chunks.
Cluster (Gaussian mixture on reduced vectors).
Summarise each cluster with an LLM and embed the summary.
Repeat until one root or a size limit.
Search the flat collection of all nodes, or traverse top-down.
trade_offs: Many LLM calls at ingest.
The tree is static: a new document may require a rebuild.

worked_example.spec: Compare with GraphRAG community summaries (same idea on a graph). Run on the 138 real passages with a local model: phase 2.

topics.title: HNSW graph index (data-side view)
topics.what_it_is: HNSW builds layers of proximity graphs. A search starts at the top sparse layer, moves greedily toward the query, and drops to the dense bottom layer. Insert adds a node with M links per layer.
topics.why: It gives high recall at low latency and supports incremental inserts, which is why it is the default in many vector databases.

symbols.l: maximum layer of an inserted node

formulas.verified: verified: HNSW Alg. 1 line 4 and mL = 1/ln(M) (Section 4)

steps: Draw the max layer of the new node.
Greedy descent from the entry point to that layer.
On each layer, search efConstruction candidates and link the M best.
Query: descend, then beam search with efSearch on layer 0.
trade_offs: Memory: the graph links add to the vectors (RAM-bound).
Deletes are awkward (tombstones).
Recall depends on efSearch.

worked_example.spec: Existing real HNSW experiment: 138 passages, M=16, efConstruction=200, k=10; at efSearch 10 recall 0.9833 and at 24 recall 0.9958 (values read from hnsw_experiment.json, small run).

topics.title: Updating the index: inserts, deletes, re-embedding
topics.what_it_is: Documents change. New text needs inserts; removed text needs deletes; a new embedding model needs a full re-embed because vectors from different models are not comparable.
topics.why: Stale or deleted content in answers is a data problem, not a model problem.
steps: Detect changes (hash per chunk).
Re-chunk and re-embed only changed documents.
Insert new vectors; mark old ones deleted.
Compact the index when tombstones exceed a threshold.
Re-embed everything when the model changes; build the new index beside the old one and switch.
trade_offs: Graph indexes degrade after many deletes (FreshDiskANN addresses this).
Chunk ids must be stable across re-chunking or links break.

worked_example.spec: Hash the 138 real passages; edit one passage; show that 1 chunk (not 138) re-embeds: arithmetic on the real corpus, demo in phase 2.

topics.title: The whole ingestion pipeline (map)
topics.what_it_is: Source files go through parse, clean, chunk, enrich with metadata, embed, index, and monitor. Each stage can lose information; the later stages cannot recover it.

steps: Parse.
Clean and deduplicate.
Chunk.
Attach metadata and lineage.
Embed.
Index.
Evaluate recall on a test set; schedule refresh.
trade_offs: Errors compound: a parser error cannot be fixed by a better embedding model.

topics.title: IVF: inverted file over clusters
topics.what_it_is: k-means splits the vectors into nlist clusters. A query visits only the nprobe nearest clusters and scans their members.
topics.why: It cuts the scanned vectors from N to about N*nprobe/nlist. Recall drops when the true neighbour sits in an unvisited cluster.
steps: Train k-means on a sample.
Assign every vector to its nearest centroid.
At query time rank centroids; take nprobe nearest.
Scan those lists; return the best k.
trade_offs: Retrain when data drifts.
Recall versus nprobe is the main knob.

worked_example.spec: Use the existing real IVF-PQ example.

topics.title: Late chunking (embed first, chunk after)
topics.what_it_is: Run a long-context embedding model over the whole document once, so every token vector has seen the full text. Then cut the token vectors into chunks and mean-pool each chunk. Each chunk vector keeps context from the rest of the document.
topics.why: It fixes the loss of context at a chunk boundary, for example a pronoun such as 'it' that refers to a subject in an earlier chunk, without calling an LLM.

io.input: whole document (up to the model context limit)

symbols.h_t: contextual token embedding from the transformer run on the full document

formulas.verified: verified: Gunther 2024 text: chunk embeddings via mean pooling of the token embeddings after encoding the whole text

steps: Tokenise the whole document within the model context.
Run the transformer once to get token vectors.
Find chunk boundaries (any strategy).
Mean-pool token vectors inside each boundary.
Index the pooled vectors.
trade_offs: Needs a long-context embedding model.
Document length is limited by the context window; use windows for longer text.

worked_example.spec: Take two adjacent real passages with a pronoun; compare cosine between chunk vector and a query with and without late chunking. Needs a long-context model (e.g. jina embeddings v2/v3), run in phase 2.

topics.demo_hint: Show token vectors, then pooled chunks.

topics.title: Learned sparse embeddings (SPLADE)
topics.what_it_is: A sparse model maps text to a vector with one weight per vocabulary word. It expands the text with related words and keeps only a few non-zero weights, so a normal inverted index can store it.
topics.why: It keeps the exact-term strength of BM25 and adds semantic expansion, in one inverted index.

symbols.h_i: contextual vector of input token i
symbols.E_j: input embedding of vocabulary word j
symbols.w_ij: importance of word j at position i
symbols.w_j: weight of word j (sum over input tokens)

formulas.verified: verified: SPLADE Eq. 1, 4 and dot-product score (text near Eq. 3)

steps: Run a masked-language-model head over the text.
Apply ReLU and log(1+x).
Max-pool over positions to get a vocabulary vector.
Sparsify with an L1 (FLOPS) regulariser.
Store in an inverted index.
trade_offs: Index size and latency depend on regularisation.
Vocabulary is model specific.

worked_example.spec: Run SPLADE on 5 real queries and print the top expanded terms; compare with BM25 matches. Phase 2.

topics.title: LLM-driven chunking (LumberChunker, Meta-Chunking)
topics.what_it_is: A language model decides where one topic ends: it reads a window of paragraphs and says where the content shifts. Meta-Chunking uses model perplexity and logical connection between sentences to place cuts.
topics.why: It finds boundaries that rules and similarity thresholds miss, especially in narrative text.
steps: Group sequential paragraphs into a window.
Ask the model where content changes (LumberChunker) or compute perplexity dips (Meta-Chunking).
Cut at that point; slide the window on.
Embed the chunks.
trade_offs: Many LLM calls at ingest; cost grows with corpus size.
Results depend on the model and prompt.

worked_example.spec: Count LLM calls for the real corpus (138 passages): one call per window; no numbers invented. Run only with a local model.

topics.title: Embedding dimension, Matryoshka truncation and storage cost
topics.what_it_is: A normal embedding must be used at its full size. A Matryoshka model is trained so that the first m dimensions already form a good embedding. You can cut the vector to 64, 128 or 256 dimensions and keep most of the quality.
topics.why: Index memory and search time grow with dimension. Truncating cuts both without retraining.
steps: Train with the loss summed over nested prefixes.
At index time choose m by budget.
Cut the vector to the first m values and re-normalise.
Optionally rerank with the full vector.
trade_offs: Only models trained this way truncate well; cutting a normal model loses quality.
Quality loss grows at very small m.

worked_example.spec: Real size: 138 vectors x 384 dims x 4 bytes = 211,968 bytes (207.0 KiB) recomputed. At 128 dims this is 70,656 bytes (one third), recomputed. Quality at 128 dims needs a Matryoshka model: not measured.

topics.title: Multi-vector retrieval (late interaction)
topics.what_it_is: ColBERT keeps one vector per token for each passage. The score sums, for each query token, its best match among the passage tokens (MaxSim).
topics.why: It matches term by term, so it keeps fine detail that one pooled vector loses, at the price of storing many vectors.

symbols.E_q_i: normalised vector of query token i
symbols.E_d_j: normalised vector of document token j

formulas.verified: verified: ColBERT Eq. 3 (S_q,d = sum_i max_j E_qi . E_dj^T)

steps: Encode every passage into token vectors offline.
Encode the query into token vectors.
Retrieve candidates by ANN search per query token.
Compute MaxSim on candidates and rank.
trade_offs: Storage: tokens x dim per passage; ColBERTv2 compresses residuals to cut it.
Needs a multi-vector aware index.

topics.title: Multimodal embeddings (text, image, page images)
topics.what_it_is: CLIP trains an image encoder and a text encoder into one space. ColPali embeds a page image directly into token-level vectors, so a scanned page can be retrieved without OCR.
topics.why: Charts, scans and slides lose meaning in text parsing. Embedding the page image keeps layout.

io.input: image or page image, plus a text query

symbols.s_ij: cosine of image i and text j

formulas.verified: verified in part: CLIP optimises a symmetric cross-entropy over the N x N similarities (text); explicit form is from the pseudocode logic

steps: Encode images and texts into one space.
Train with a symmetric contrastive loss.
For page retrieval: split the page into patches and keep patch vectors.
Score with MaxSim (ColPali).
trade_offs: Larger index than text-only.
Quality on dense text pages still trails strong OCR pipelines in some cases (not measured here).

topics.title: Parent-document / small-to-big retrieval
topics.what_it_is: Embed small chunks (sentences or propositions) for precise matching, then return the larger parent (paragraph or section) to the LLM. The index holds small vectors; the context holds big text.
topics.why: Small units match a query better. Large units give the LLM enough context. This decouples the unit of search from the unit of reading.

io.output: parent text for each matched child

steps: Cut parents (sections) then children (sentences).
Embed children; store child->parent id.
Search children; collect parent ids; deduplicate.
Return parents, ranked by best child score.
trade_offs: Several hits in one parent waste context if not deduplicated.
Parents that are too large bring noise back.

worked_example.spec: On the real chunk-size data: embedding at 20 words and reading at 120 words is the combination to test; the experiment file measures only equal sizes, so this is a new run (phase 2).

topics.title: Product quantization (PQ)
topics.what_it_is: Split a d-dimensional vector into m sub-vectors. For each part, a k-means codebook of 256 centroids is learned. A vector is stored as m one-byte codes. Distances are computed from small lookup tables.
topics.why: It compresses vectors 10 to 100 times, so billions fit in RAM, at a small recall loss.

formulas.verified: NOT verified: Jegou 2010 PDF not retrievable (HAL copy blocked)

steps: Split vectors into m parts.
Learn a 256-centroid codebook per part.
Encode each vector as m bytes.
At query time build m lookup tables.
Sum table entries per vector.
trade_offs: Distortion grows with compression; rerank the top candidates with full vectors.

worked_example.spec: 384-d float32 vector = 1,536 bytes. With m=48 one-byte codes = 48 bytes: 32x smaller (recomputed). Real PQ run: existing real-ivf_pq.json.

topics.title: Proposition chunking
topics.what_it_is: An LLM rewrites each passage into propositions: short, self-contained statements with names resolved (no pronouns). Each proposition is embedded as a chunk.
topics.why: Each unit holds one fact and needs no outside context, which makes dense retrieval precise.
steps: Prompt (or fine-tune) a model to split a passage into atomic facts.
Decontextualise: replace pronouns by names.
Embed each proposition.
Index with a link to the source passage.
trade_offs: Costs an LLM call per passage at ingest.
Rewriting can introduce errors that the source text did not have.

worked_example.spec: Run propositionizer on 5 real corpus passages; count propositions per passage; check each against the source by hand. Needs a model call: use a local model (no paid LLM).

topics.title: Recursive character / separator chunking
topics.what_it_is: Try to split on the largest separator first (section break, then paragraph, then sentence, then word). If a piece is still too long, split it with the next separator. Result: chunks near the target size that mostly follow the text structure.
topics.why: It is the default splitter in common RAG libraries and a strong baseline.
steps: Split by the first separator.
Merge small neighbours up to the size limit.
For pieces over the limit, recurse with the next separator.
Add overlap if wanted.
trade_offs: Depends on clean separators; poorly parsed text has none.

worked_example.spec: Run on the real corpus passages at 40 and 80 words and compare chunk counts with fixed-size. To be computed in phase 2.

topics.title: Semantic chunking (embedding or lexical breakpoints)
topics.what_it_is: Embed each sentence. Cut where the similarity between neighbouring sentences (or blocks) drops below a threshold. Chunks then follow topic shifts.
topics.why: It tries to keep one idea per chunk. It costs one embedding per sentence at ingest.

symbols.e_i: embedding of sentence i (or window of sentences)
symbols.d_i: cosine distance to the next sentence
symbols.mu_d, sigma_d: mean and standard deviation of d

formulas.verified: inferred rule, not from a paper (TextTiling uses a depth score over a lexical similarity curve: verified in the Hearst PDF)

steps: Split into sentences.
Embed each sentence (optionally with neighbours).
Compute distances between neighbours.
Cut at distances above the threshold (percentile or z-score).
Merge or split chunks to respect size limits.
trade_offs: Qu 2024 finds the extra cost not consistently justified against fixed-size chunks.
Short sentences give noisy embeddings.
Threshold needs tuning per corpus.

worked_example.spec: Use vectors_sample.json: the cosine matrix of 6 real sentences (s1-s2 = 0.5408, recomputed from the normalised vectors = 0.5408) shows the adjacent-similarity values a chunker would threshold. Full run on the corpus is a phase-2 task.

introduced_by.title: TextTiling: Segmenting Text into Multi-paragraph Subtopic Passages
introduced_by.why: Splits text where lexical similarity between adjacent blocks drops (a depth score over a similarity curve): the ancestor of embedding-based semantic chunking.

also_cite.why: Empirical test of semantic chunkers against fixed-size ones; finds the benefit inconsistent for the cost.

provenance.notes: The embedding-breakpoint form of semantic chunking was popularised in practitioner notebooks and libraries; no peer-reviewed origin found in this pass (unverified). TextTiling is the verified ancestor.

topics.title: Structure-aware chunking (headings, tables, code, pages)
topics.what_it_is: Use the parsed document tree: one chunk per section, table, list or code block, with the heading path attached. Long sections are split further.
topics.why: Chunks follow the author's own structure, and the heading path becomes metadata that helps retrieval and citation.

io.output: chunks with heading path, page and element type

steps: Parse to a tree (Docling, Nougat, HTML DOM).
Walk the tree; keep tables and code whole when possible.
Prepend the heading path to the chunk text.
Split oversized nodes recursively.
trade_offs: Needs a good parser.
Very uneven chunk sizes.

topics.title: Table structure recognition
topics.what_it_is: A table-structure model finds rows, columns and merged cells in a table image or region and outputs a grid. The grid keeps each cell with its row and column header.
topics.why: A table turned into a text line loses which number belongs to which header. A grid lets the chunker keep a row with its headers.

io.output: grid of cells with row/column spans and header flags

steps: Crop the table region found by the layout model.
Encode the image with a CNN backbone and a transformer encoder.
Decode the table structure as a token sequence (HTML-like tags).
Predict a bounding box for each cell and match it to the PDF text.
Export cells to Markdown, CSV or JSON.
trade_offs: Borderless tables and nested tables remain hard.
Very large tables exceed chunk limits: split by rows and repeat the header.

worked_example.spec: Take one real table from a PDF, run docling, check cell count against the page by eye. Not in the real-example pack yet.

topics.title: Tokenisation (subword units)
topics.what_it_is: Before a transformer reads text, a tokenizer splits it into subword tokens from a fixed vocabulary (WordPiece, BPE). Rare words become several pieces; each piece has an integer id.
topics.why: Token limits decide chunk size, cost and truncation. Different models have different tokenizers, so token counts differ.

io.output: list of token ids (plus special tokens)

symbols.(x,y): adjacent symbol pair in the training corpus

formulas.verified: verified: Sennrich 2016 iteratively merges the most frequent pair of symbols (BPE)

steps: Normalise text (case, accents).
Split into words, then into subwords by the learned merges.
Map pieces to ids; add [CLS]/[SEP].
Truncate or pad to the model limit.
trade_offs: Silent truncation drops the tail of long chunks.
Numbers, code and non-Latin scripts may split into many tokens.

worked_example.spec: Real numbers from the chunk-size experiment (all-MiniLM-L6-v2, 256-token limit): chunks over 256 tokens: 0 at 20 and 40 words, 3 at 80, 2 at 120, 218 at 200, 165 at 300 target words. So 200-word chunks are mostly truncated by this model (values read from chunking_experiment.json).

topics.title: Versioning, lineage and provenance of chunks
topics.what_it_is: Each chunk keeps source id, source version, parser version, chunker settings and embedding model id. This record is the lineage of a vector.
topics.why: Without it you cannot say which text produced an answer or which vectors are stale after a parser or model change.
steps: Record source revision id (oldid), parser and version, chunker parameters, model id and date.
Store the record as chunk metadata.
On pipeline change, select affected chunks by lineage and re-process.
Show the lineage in the citation.
trade_offs: More metadata means more storage and a stricter schema.

worked_example.spec: Pack passages already carry oldid and retrieved date: show them as lineage.
